rv.q: Rebeck's new play is seldom predictable and never boring, and her cast, led by Norbert Leo Butz, glitters like sapphires on black velvet.
None of these actors, though, can help the lack of credibility of some of the play's central devices.
The play is funny, just not uproarious enough to hide its lack of substance or consistency.
Rebeck has stumbled a bit with 'Dead Accounts,' a love letter to the hardworking, plainspoken Midwest, but one that lacks the sharpness and depth of her previous work.

Butz practically ricochets off the walls of the simple Midwestern kitchen that’s the setting for “Dead Accounts,” but not even he can transcend the contrived nature of a character who is really nothing more than a collection of manic playwriting impulses.
Any analysis of the chemical makeup of Norbert Leo Butz would surely reveal traces of gunpowder.

But how did Holmes and a bushel of theater talents, including director Jack O'Brien, take a wrong turn into this slim screech of a sitcom, a scattershot slice of stereotypical life with characters as unbelievable as they are unlikeable?
A full season (or further re-writing) might have allowed Rebeck to flesh out her promising setup, but this wisp of a show pays steep penalties for premature withdrawal.

And in "Dead Accounts," a thin and annoyingly glib comedy that opened Thursday night at the Theatre, he gamely draws on every facet of his impishly outrageous stage persona – he's compulsive, wheedling, devious – in portraying a crooked banker named Jack.
There's 'Dead Accounts' and then there's 'No Accounts'
“Dead Accounts,” on the other hand, seems phoned in, the kind of TV sitcom Rebeck herself can tear into with delicious spleen.

cn.t: Critics pan Rebeck's thin, dramatically lifeless comedy, though Norbert Leo Butz earns widespread praise for his energetic performance. Holmes receives mixed notices in this widely dismissed Broadway misfire.

vs.sum: The Music Box Theatre offers excellent sightlines from most seats, making it ideal for intimate dramas, though sound quality can vary. The theater's charming Georgian-inspired design adds to its ambiance, while comfort and facilities are average for a Broadway venue.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
